source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Autobiographical reflection on the years of struggle

source.excerpt: I learned that courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it. I felt fear myself more times than I can remember, but I hid it behind a mask of boldness. The brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear.
trail: The line appears in Mandela’s autobiography Long Walk to Freedom ↗, first published in 1994.
The official Nelson Mandela page ↗ cites the full passage as from that book, dated 1994.
The broader aphorism predates him: Mark Twain’s Pudd’nhead Wilson ↗ (1894) called courage “mastery of fear—not absence of fear.”
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version quotes only the first sentence
source.excerptNote: The widely-shared version keeps only the opening sentence; the fuller passage adds Mandela’s admission that he too felt fear and merely “hid it behind a mask of boldness.”
source.rightsNote: “Long Walk to Freedom” (1994) remains under copyright; this excerpt is quoted for identification and comment. The quotation itself is Mandela’s and is not in the public domain.

author.name: Nelson Mandela
author.heading: About Nelson Mandela
author.bio: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela spent 27 years in prison for his role in the fight against apartheid before walking free in 1990 and becoming South Africa’s first democratically elected President in 1994. His autobiography, Long Walk to Freedom — begun in secret on Robben Island in 1976 and completed with journalist Richard Stengel — is the primary source for many of his most-quoted reflections, including this one on courage and fear.

misattribution.heading: A note on origins
misattribution.intro: Mandela is correctly credited — the sentence really is his, published under his name in his own memoir. What gets muddled is the assumption that he originated the idea. The insight that courage is not the absence of fear is considerably older, so the aphorism is sometimes handed instead to earlier voices.

items.why: Twain’s Pudd’nhead Wilson ↗ (1894) reads “Courage is resistance to fear, mastery of fear—not absence of fear” — the same insight, but distinct wording that predates Mandela by a century.

Redmoon’s 1991 essay “No Peaceful Warriors!” wrote “Courage is not the absence of fear, but rather the judgment that something else is more important than one’s fear,” per this origins investigation ↗ — also predating Mandela’s 1994 book.

misattribution.truthLine: The specific line — “courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it” — is Mandela’s own, from Long Walk to Freedom ↗ (1994); the underlying idea is simply older than the phrasing.

context.heading: Why it resonated
lead: Coming from a man who spent 27 years imprisoned, the words carry an authority few speakers could claim. Mandela does not present himself as fearless; he confesses to feeling fear “more times than I can remember” and admits he simply masked it. That candor is what makes the line land: courage is reframed as something ordinary people can practice, not a gift reserved for the naturally unafraid.
detailsBody: Long Walk to Freedom was drafted by Mandela on Robben Island and later completed with the help of journalist Richard Stengel. Collaborative authorship is standard for political memoirs, and the book is published under Mandela’s name as his own account — so the line is properly attributed to him, even as the underlying aphorism about fear and courage has older antecedents.
